responses: After careful consideration of the group’s discussions, my final position is that we should allocate 35% to Workforce Training, 25% to Automation, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 10% to Employee Support, and 10% to the Innovation Lab. I believe this balance prioritizes our people first—ensuring they are equipped and supported through the transition—while still making meaningful investments in automation and the foundational data systems needed to sustain long-term efficiency and growth. The Innovation Lab and Employee Support, while valuable, should receive smaller shares to avoid spreading our $5 million budget too thin across too many fronts.

I would recommend a balanced allocation that prioritizes Workforce Training (30%) and Employee Support (20%) alongside Automation (25%), with the remainder going to Data Infrastructure (15%) and Innovation Lab (10%). The human side of this transition is critical—without reskilling and support, automation investments risk creating resistance, turnover, and morale problems that undermine long-term gains. At the same time, we can't ignore the competitive pressure to modernize manufacturing, so a significant automation investment is necessary. Data infrastructure provides the foundation for both automation and innovation, while the Innovation Lab keeps us experimenting for future growth. This approach mitigates risk by not over-investing in any single area while ensuring employees feel valued and prepared for change.

I’d tell them that after a lot of back-and-forth, I came to see that the smartest move isn’t to go all-in on automation or just throw money at training—it’s about balance. I ended up pushing for a solid chunk of the budget to go toward workforce training and employee support, because if we don’t help people adapt and feel secure, the new tech will just create resentment and turnover. At the same time, I think we need to invest enough in data infrastructure and a smaller innovation lab to actually build the foundation for long-term change, while keeping automation at a measured pace so we don’t disrupt operations too fast. In short, it’s about treating the transition as a human challenge first, with technology as the tool—not the goal.

After careful consideration of the committee’s discussions, my final position is that we should allocate the $5 million budget with a strong emphasis on **Workforce Training (35%)** and **Employee Support (25%)**, followed by **Data Infrastructure (20%)**, **Automation (15%)**, and a smaller **Innovation Lab (5%)**. I believe that rushing into automation without adequately preparing our people would be a critical mistake—our employees are the backbone of Riverton, and their anxiety about job displacement is real. By investing heavily in reskilling, AI literacy, and mental health support, we can build trust and ensure a smoother transition. Data infrastructure is essential to support any AI tools we deploy, but it should not come at the cost of neglecting our workforce. Automation should be phased in gradually, and the Innovation Lab can remain a modest experimental space. This balanced approach prioritizes human capital while still moving the company forward technologically.

I'd recommend a balanced but forward-leaning allocation: 30% to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 15% to Innovation Lab, and 10% to Employee Support. Automation gives us immediate competitive gains and efficiency, which justifies the largest share. But without training and support, we risk alienating our workforce—so investing in reskilling and transition assistance is essential for morale and retention. Data infrastructure is the backbone that makes automation and innovation work, so it needs significant funding. The Innovation Lab keeps us future-focused, while Employee Support ensures we handle the human side of change responsibly. This mix balances short-term results with long-term adaptability and employee well-being.

I’d tell them that after all the discussion, I came down firmly in favor of putting the largest share—about 35%—into workforce training, because no matter how good the AI tools are, they’re useless if people don’t know how to use them or feel threatened by them. I’d also allocate 25% to data infrastructure, since that’s the foundation everything else runs on, and 20% to automation to stay competitive, but only at a measured pace. The remaining 20% would split between the innovation lab and employee support, because we need to experiment with new ideas and also help people through the transition without burning them out. In short, I’d say the smartest investment is in our people first, then the systems that empower them.

After careful consideration of our discussions, I believe the most balanced and responsible allocation is to prioritize **Workforce Training (35%)** and **Employee Support (25%)** as the foundation of our AI transition, ensuring our people are equipped and supported through the change, while dedicating **Automation (20%)** to targeted efficiency gains, **Data Infrastructure (15%)** to build the necessary technical backbone, and a smaller **Innovation Lab (5%)** for exploratory R&D. This approach recognizes that our greatest asset is our workforce—without their buy-in and skills, the technology will fail—and that a gradual, human-centered transition will yield more sustainable long-term results than rushing into automation at the expense of employee morale and adaptability.
